The natural outcome would have been razzone [rat'tsone] (which is attested in some archaic works in Roman vernacular); the reason why the modern form shows a g is that Tuscan literates mistook Northern rason as an outcome of non-existent Latin **rasione~**raseone—whose -sj- indeed evolves regularly into tuscan [ʃ]~[ʒ] and non-tuscan [s]<s> (compare fagiolo from Latin phaseolum, and compare the pronunciation of English vision as "vizhun"—indeed, approvvigionare ultimately comes from Latin visionem with the same assimilation of -sj- into a palatal voiced fricative). Compare other terms ending in -gione. Furthermore, the reason why it’s nowadays pronounced with an affricate rather than a fricative (together with all Italian terms having as the corresponding etymological clusters being -tj- or -sj-, or even -cj- through Gallic languages—see crogiolo) is due to hyper-correction of Tuscan gorgia, i.e. the merging of ungeminated fricatives and affricates into the first ones. Indeed, older spellings with sci or sgi tried to reproduce the ungeminated fricative before the gorgia took place (once it happened, it was more convenient, with merged sounds, to merge the spellings, despite being unetymological).

c. 1300, as masculine razzo, the feminine razza is from the early 14th century. The etymology of this word is uncertain, with a large number of controversially discussed suggestions.
Among the most widely accepted suggestions is the one embraced by Französisches Etymologisches Wörterbuch (1922), but was proposed earlier, among others by L. Spitzer (Z. rom. Philol. t. 53, pp. 300–301), which derives the word from Latin ratiō (the nominative, as opposed to ragione, from the accusative ratiōnem, which nonetheless was attested with a similar sense to razza in the late Middle Ages; ratio also came to mean “idea” or “conception of something” in Ecclesiastical Latin) likely via a Vulgar Latin variant *ratia, and underwent a change of gender later from an original form *razzo, or else derived ultimately from generātiō through apheresis.
Another likely origin is from the Latin racēmus, meaning a “cluster or bunch of grapes, berries or similar fruits”, from which the French “raisin” is derived.
Other suggestions include, Lombardic *raiza (compare Old High German reiza (“line”)), Latin rādīx (“root”) or Ancient Greek ῥίζα (rhíza, “root”), Arabic رَأْس (raʔs, “head”), or Old French haraz (“culture of horses”).
